study_order: Study order. Chapters 1–2 set the ground rules: course logistics, the number-systems refresher every later chapter leans on, and the ethics and law that separate a security professional from a criminal. Chapter 3 is the conceptual core (CIA, threats and attacks, the first look at cryptography, passwords, and access control) and carries your professor's “worth notice” list, marked ★ in its exam checklist. Chapter 4 is the math-heavy one: block ciphers, modes, RSA, and hashing. Chapters 5–6 apply everything to operating systems, first UNIX and then Windows, and Chapter 7 goes down to the memory level with buffer overflows, where C's missing bounds checks turn a programming mistake into attacker-controlled code. Chapter 8 is the catalogue of what gets run once a bug like that is exploited — malware, organised along two axes, how it propagates and what its payload does — and Chapter 9 moves outward to the network, first teaching how the Internet actually works and then showing that ARP, IP, DNS, TCP, and BGP were all designed with no authentication at all. Chapter 10 turns to defence — firewalls, intrusion detection, VPNs, and the zero-trust argument that the perimeter they all assume no longer holds. The course is cumulative, so earlier chapters stay fair game on later exams. The formula sheet at the back collects every formula in one place.
